<user_query>
can rust and go work well tegether?
</user_query>
Rust and Go work well together when each owns a clear boundary. I’ll check whether this repo already mixes them so the answer matches your project.

Yes. Rust and Go work well together as **separate programs that talk over a network or a queue**. They are a poor fit inside one process.

This repo is Rust only (`shippin.tech` and its crates). There is no Go code here today.

**What works well**

- **HTTP or gRPC.** Each side owns its own binary. Rust handles the hot path (mail I/O, storage, parsing). Go handles glue: admin APIs, workers, CLIs, or a control plane.
- **A broker you already depend on.** This project can build with NATS or Kafka. Either language can publish and consume without linking the other runtime.
- **A shared store.** Postgres, Redis, or object storage is a clean contract. Neither side needs to know the other’s memory model.
- **A CLI boundary.** One binary shells out to the other for a batch job. Simple, and failure stays in that process.

**What is awkward**

Calling Rust from Go (or the reverse) through cgo / a C ABI works, but you pay for it: extra build steps, a C toolchain, slower calls, and harder crashes to debug. Use that only for a small, stable library with a C-shaped API. Do not split a request handler across both languages in one process.

**Practical split**

| Rust | Go |
|---|---|
| SMTP, IMAP, JMAP, storage, spam filtering | Operators, dashboards, one-off workers, SDKs |
| Tight latency and memory control | Fast iteration and straightforward concurrency |

Ship two binaries, version the API between them, and keep retries and timeouts at that boundary. That is the combination that stays easy to deploy and debug.

<timestamp>Wednesday, Oct 28, 2026, 8:29 AM (UTC-7)</timestamp>
<user_query>
but is it worth it or can mail now be done fully in rust or as a cloud service is go the better language or a hybrid like i am thinking
</user_query>
The choice depends on what you keep in this Rust server and what a cloud product still has to add. I’ll look at what shippin already covers so the recommendation matches the codebase.

Mail itself can be done fully in Rust, and this tree already does it. A hybrid is worth it only for the cloud product around that engine. Go should not be a second mail server.

The README’s “expand off Mox” split is the expensive version. Mox is a complete Go mail server aimed at one operator and one machine. This repo is already the other complete server: SMTP, IMAP, JMAP, POP3, ManageSieve, CalDAV/CardDAV, directory, spam filtering, object storage, and a cluster coordinator (NATS, Kafka, Redis, Zenoh). Running both means two MTAs, two stores, and two places a message can get lost. That is the mailcow problem (Postfix plus Dovecot plus Rspamd plus SOGo), not the modernization of it.

**Use Rust for the daemon you already have.** Receiving, parsing, filtering, storing, and serving mail is the hot path. Rewriting it in Go throws away the crates in this workspace. Go can run a mail server — Mox proves that — but it is not a better language for this daemon once the Rust one exists.

**Use Go for the cloud shell mailcow users actually feel.** That is a different program:

- signup, domains, mailboxes, aliases, app passwords
- SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks, plus certificate issuance
- plans, quotas, billing
- the admin API and web UI
- install, Compose, or a Kubernetes operator

That shell should provision this server over its HTTP admin API. It should not parse MIME or speak SMTP.

**When the hybrid pays off.** You want a mailcow-style hosted product, and the panel will move faster in Go than in Rust. Keep the contract narrow: Go decides who exists and what their quota is; Rust delivers the mail.

**When it does not.** A small team shipping the server itself. A second language, a second build, and a second on-call skill cost more than they save. Build the admin API in the existing Rust `http` and `directory` crates and stay in one binary until the panel is a real product.

So: one mail engine, in Rust. Go only as the control plane in front of it. Leave Mox out.

<timestamp>Wednesday, Oct 28, 2026, 8:31 AM (UTC-7)</timestamp>
<user_query>
i know this can do mail somewhat already ive been building it but I need to decide like part of me really thinks that mox might be worth my time but never seen or used it and this really does run optimized but i need it to be zoho mail opensourced i think
</user_query>
You already have a mail engine. The Zoho-shaped question is which missing product pieces Mox would actually give you. I’ll check what this tree covers against that.

Stay on this server. Mox is worth a weekend so you can see the product you are missing. It is not worth a port if the goal is Zoho Mail, open sourced.

What feels attractive about Mox is real. It is one Go binary that already feels like a product: webmail, an admin page, automatic TLS, and SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS, and DANE wired in so a single domain can send and receive without a stack of containers. This tree does not feel like that. It is an engine. You have been feeling a product gap, and Mox is the open-source server that hides that gap for a small host.

Zoho Mail is the other shape. An organization signs up, adds a domain, creates users, aliases, and groups, and lives in a web client that also has calendar and contacts. Admins set policy. Phones use IMAP or JMAP. The service hosts many of those organizations. That is a client plus an org control plane sitting on a mail and groupware engine.

You already have the engine Zoho needs, and Mox does not:

- JMAP mail, plus calendar and contacts
- CalDAV and CardDAV, including scheduling
- IMAP, SMTP, POP3, and Sieve
- directory, quotas, ACLs, OAuth
- spam filtering, object storage, and a cluster coordinator

Mox will not grow into that without you writing those systems again in Go. You would be trading an optimized backend for a self-host UI aimed at one operator.

The Zoho-shaped work left on this repo is the product, and there is no webmail app in this tree today (only login and calendar-invite templates):

| Zoho piece | Where it should live |
|---|---|
| Inbox, search, compose, threads, attachments | A JMAP web client |
| Calendar and contacts in the same login | Same client, on the JMAP and CalDAV you have |
| Org, domain, users, aliases, groups | A Go or Rust admin app over the directory API |
| DNS and DKIM setup | That admin app. Steal Mox’s flow here |
| Spam the user can review | A quarantine view on the existing filter |
| Phone clients | IMAP and SMTP you already serve |
| Retention, eDiscovery, Streams, native mobile apps | Later |

Run Mox once and watch only three things: the first-domain setup, the webmail, and the DNS and deliverability screens. Copy those into an admin and a web client in front of this server. Leave Mox’s SMTP and IMAP where they are.

You want a growth plan for an open shippin.tech, with shippin.cloud as the later hosted product. I’ll read the planning approach and the repo’s current shape so the plan matches what you already have.
The open-source boundary is the decision that shapes everything else. I’ll check the license and what the enterprise flags actually lock before laying out a growth plan.

Ship the same mail server to everyone, and let shippin.cloud charge for running it. The code you write is AGPL. The Stalwart Enterprise License snippets already in this tree stay out of the public build until you replace them with your own.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` already says AGPL-3.0. `Cargo.toml` still says the license is "deciding." A large set of features is marked `LicenseRef-SEL` and wrapped in `feature = "enterprise"`: tenant quotas, SCIM, sharding and read replicas, telemetry, archiving, masked email, and the LLM spam path. Those snippets are not yours to relicense. The public shippin.tech build is the AGPL server with that feature off. shippin.cloud does not need a private mail daemon. It needs accounts, billing, and machines.

**What you are building**

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| shippin.tech | The brand, the site, and the open product people download |
| This repo | The Rust mail and groupware engine |
| A new web app | Inbox, calendar, and contacts. This is the part that feels like Zoho |
| shippin.cloud | Paid hosting of that same AGPL build, later |

Go waits. It becomes useful when cloud signup has to provision many servers. Mox stays a weekend of clicking through setup and webmail, then you copy the ideas.

**Phase 1. One open server you can hand to someone.** Put `AGPL-3.0` in `Cargo.toml` and add a `LICENSE` file for your code. Change the default build so it is RocksDB without `enterprise`. Write a README that says this is a mail, calendar, and contacts server. Add a Compose file that boots one node with one domain and one mailbox. Done means a stranger clones the repo, runs Compose, and sends a message to that mailbox over SMTP and IMAP.

**Phase 2. The product people live in.** A React app on JMAP: inbox, search, compose, threads, attachments, calendar, and contacts, one login. Phone clients keep using the IMAP and SMTP you already serve. Done means you can work a day in the browser without opening Thunderbird.

**Phase 3. The admin a small company expects.** Domains, users, aliases, groups, quotas, and a DKIM, SPF, and DMARC setup screen. It talks to the directory and registry APIs you already have. This is the screen worth studying in Mox. Done means a new domain receives mail without editing a config file by hand.

**Phase 4. shippin.cloud.** A separate control plane creates an account, starts the same AGPL binary, and points a domain at it. Billing and the trademark live here. The mailbox data stays in the engine. AI comes after that, as a side panel using the user's own JMAP session and a key they bring. A hosted model can be a cloud convenience. It is not a closed mail feature.

**Leave closed, on purpose.** The SEL-marked code, until you rewrite a piece and add it to the AGPL build. Payment processing. The shippin.tech and shippin.cloud names, which stay your trademark even though the code is open.

**Rewrite only when the open product is blocked.** First originals worth writing are per-organization quotas and user directory sync, because SCIM and tenant limits are behind the enterprise flag today. Clustering and the LLM filter can wait.

I have not changed any files. If this split is the one you want, the first implementation pass is Phase 1 only: license file, default features, README, and Compose.

Enterprise came off the build because I treated the license as already decided. You have not decided that. I’ll check exactly what Rocks and the enterprise flag do in this tree, then put the build back so Rocks stays supported and enterprise is not dropped ahead of that choice.

Rocks is the single-machine database. Enterprise is a separate block of code, and it is back on the default build. Taking it off was a license decision, and you have not made that decision.

**Rocks** is RocksDB, compiled by the `rocks` feature as `DataStore::RocksDb`. Mail, calendar, and directory rows sit in one directory on one disk (`RocksDbStore.path`). There is no second server in that setup. A second process with its own directory has its own mailboxes. That is why a cluster does not use Rocks as the shared store. The scale build still compiles Rocks, so a one-node server keeps using it. Shared mail across nodes is FoundationDB for the data, S3 for the blobs, and NATS or Redis so the nodes hear each other.

**Enterprise** is the `enterprise` feature. It turns on the blocks marked `LicenseRef-SEL`: tenant quotas, SCIM, sharded stores, the composite backend, and the LLM filter. It is not a storage engine and it is not required for Rocks. I took it off `default` and both Dockerfiles because an earlier pass treated AGPL as chosen and treated those blocks as forbidden in the public binary. You have moved off that. `Cargo.toml` still says the license is `"deciding"`.

I put `enterprise` back on the default features and on both Dockerfiles. `scale` now includes Rocks plus FoundationDB, S3, Redis, and NATS. `cargo build --features scale` keeps Rocks and enterprise and adds the shared-store backends.

I read “bgl” as the Business Source License. That is the license that publishes the source and can reserve competing commercial hosting for shippin.cloud until a conversion date. A true open-source license cannot reserve hosting. Those two choices are still open, and neither one is written into the repo yet.

The session protocol is the Wardenclyffe memory schema, stored as files in this repo because SurrealDB is not running here. Raw chat and the journal are different records.

| Record | What it holds | Where it goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session_event` | One raw transcript line, or one hook payload | `sessions/<id>/events.jsonl` |
| `agent_message` | User or assistant text from that line | `sessions/<id>/messages.jsonl` |
| `tool_event` | A tool call. Inputs are redacted | `sessions/<id>/tools.jsonl` |
| `reasoning_observation` | Thinking or compaction text | `sessions/<id>/reasoning.jsonl` |
| `journal_entry` | A deliberate note: hypothesis, command, result, decision, correction | `journal/journal.jsonl` |
| `lesson` | A curated gotcha, decision, convention, or anti-pattern | `journal/lessons.jsonl` |

The copier does not write the journal or the lessons. Those are self-reports, not a second copy of the chat. Hooks follow the same order as the Wardenclyffe Cursor hook: session start, prompt, tool use, tool failure, thought, response, compact, stop, session end. `beforeSubmitPrompt` returns allow. Every hook is fail-open: the spool is written first.
